summary: Updates the BGP Monitoring Protocol, which only exposed routes received from peers, to also give access to routes a router sends out. It adds a flag to the peer header to tell the received and outgoing tables apart. It updates RFC 7854.

eli5.summary: A router keeps a list of what it heard and what it will say. This lets monitors see the what-it-will-say list too, not only the heard one.

questions: what is the bmp o flag
what is pre-policy vs post-policy adj-rib-out
subtitle: Lets BGP monitoring show the routes a router advertises, not only the ones it receives.

tldr.problem: BMP only gave access to Adj-RIB-In, the routes a router received. A provider could not see what it advertises to a customer if the customer did not run BMP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8671 adds an O flag to the BMP per-peer header (0 for Adj-RIB-In, 1 for Adj-RIB-Out), defines pre-policy and post-policy Adj-RIB-Out, adds four statistics types and an Admin Label TLV for Peer Up.
tldr.outcome: A BMP sender can report what it advertises to peers, for outbound policy validation and for monitoring advertised routes. It updates RFC 7854 and is itself updated by RFC 9736.

today: RFC 8671 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7854, and it is itself updated by RFC 9736. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Monitor Adj-RIB-Out
sections.content:
The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP, RFC 7854) monitors the received Routing Information Bases (RIBs) per peer. Pre-policy Adj-RIB-In conveys the data before any policy is applied; post-policy Adj-RIB-In conveys it after policy filters or modifications.

Being limited to Adj-RIB-In is a problem when the receiving end of a BGP peering is not enabled for BMP or not accessible. For example, a service provider advertises prefixes to a customer but cannot see what it advertises, and asking the customer to enable BMP is not feasible.

RFC 8671 lets a BMP sender report what it advertises to BGP peers. The RFC says this can be used for outbound policy validation and for monitoring advertised routes.
sections.eli5: Until now you could only listen to what a router heard. This lets you also listen to what it says to others.

sections.title: Pre-policy and Post-policy Adj-RIB-Out
sections.content:
As defined in RFC 4271, the Adj-RIBs-Out contain the routes for advertisement to specific peers in the local speaker's UPDATE messages. This RFC defines two views of it.

  • Pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out: the result before outbound policy. It normally matches what is in the local RIB, though it holds only the routes available for the peering type (IBGP, route reflector client, EBGP, confederation, route server client).
  • Post-policy Adj-RIB-Out: the result after outbound policy. It MUST convey to the BMP receiver what is actually transmitted to the peer, including attributes such as next hop that are set at transmission.

Comparing the two can validate and audit outbound policy. Mandatory attributes unknown at the pre-policy stage, such as next hop, MUST be zero or have an empty length, and the BMP receiver treats them as self-originated.
sections.eli5: There are two copies of the outgoing list: one before the router's rules are applied, and one showing exactly what was sent.

sections.title: The O Flag in the Per-Peer Header
sections.content:
The per-peer header keeps the structure and flags of RFC 7854 and adds the O flag after V, L and A. O is 0 for Adj-RIB-In and 1 for Adj-RIB-Out. The remaining bits are reserved, MUST be sent as 0 and MUST be ignored on receipt.

The existing L flag still selects policy: it MUST be 1 for post-policy and 0 for pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out.

When O is 1, several fields change meaning to refer to the peer the PDU is sent to: Peer Address, Peer AS and Peer BGP ID. The Timestamp is the time the routes were advertised (or installed in the Adj-RIB-Out); zero means unavailable.
sections.eli5: One extra yes/no switch on each message says whether it describes the heard list or the will-say list.

sections.title: Effects on BMP Messages
sections.content:
Route Monitoring and Route Mirroring messages MUST set O to say whether they carry Adj-RIB-In or Adj-RIB-Out. Statistics Reports are not specific to either, so they MUST have O set to zero and the receiver SHOULD ignore it. Peer Up and Down Notifications describe session state, and receivers SHOULD ignore O in them.

Four new statistics types count routes in Adj-RIB-Out: 14 and 15 are 64-bit gauges for pre-policy and post-policy, and 16 and 17 are the per-AFI/SAFI versions, structured as a 2-byte AFI, a 1-byte SAFI and a 64-bit gauge.

A new Peer Up Information TLV, type 4 Admin Label, carries an optional free-form UTF-8 string. Several labels may appear and the receiver MUST preserve their order.
sections.eli5: Counting messages get four new counters for the outgoing list, and a router can attach sticky-note labels to each peer.

sections.title: Peer Groups and Session Changes
sections.content:
Implementations use peer and update groups for efficiency, so a single peer can represent hundreds of peers, for example wholesale peers that should never be sent routes with community X:Y. Group names are not simple because policy grouping is structured and inherited. Instead, the Admin Label lets operators tag peers, such as type=wholesale or region=west. How labels are configured and assigned is implementation-specific.

If a change alters the behavior of an existing BMP session (changes to filtering and table names), the session MUST be bounced with a Peer Down/Peer Up sequence.
sections.eli5: Instead of listing every peer, you stick labels like "wholesale" on them so you can check the whole bunch at once.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7854 apply. Implementations SHOULD require sessions with authorized and trusted monitoring devices, and the RFC believes it adds no further security considerations.

IANA assigned flag 3 (the O flag) in the BMP Peer Flags registry, Stat Types 14 to 17, and Initiation Message TLV type 4 (Admin Label).
sections.eli5: Only let trusted watchers listen in, just as before.
